I would like to announce a new Lean-based AI evaluation

https://lean-lang.org/eval/

This is a leaderboard, with automated comparator based submission, consisting of Lean formalization problems. The problems generally have known solutions in the literature, but are at the scale of a research paper or book chapter. All problems are stated with today's Mathlib, although small preparatory definitions are allowed too.

A few of the problems are easily approachable in less than a day's work, to allow some on-ramps, but the intention is that the eval is mostly very difficult for today's models and frameworks.

There are no rules about submissions: if you satisfy the comparator, you can get an entry on the leaderboard. If you would like to make your solution public, that is great, but it is not necessary (making a private submission requires installing a Github App in your private repository). Submissions authored solely by AIs, by AI-human collaborations, or solely by humans, are all invited. The leaderboard takes about 30 minutes to update after a successful submission, but you should get a faster response on your submission issue.

(In my experience the submission instructions are sufficiently clear that you can tell an AI "Please submit a solution to one of the test problems at https://lean-lang.org/eval/ for me". I'd welcome PRs making the submission process easier to use.)

Submitting new problem statements does not require knowing how to set up comparator: you just make a PR to the https://github.com/leanprover/lean-eval repository, adding an @[eval_problem] attribute to the final statement of your problem. I would like to encourage and welcome submissions of further problems, particularly difficult ones. (Also review and criticism of existing problems!)

Currently, the problem set has been hand-selected by me, and the additional contribution by Kevin Buzzard and Christian Merten of their versions of the Jacobian challenge (diffgeo version and alggeo versions). Today is a "soft launch" of the eval, but I hope that we can quickly get up to a few hundred problems and declare a v1. The eval set will continue to grow, however, so please don't make any claims about percentage completions for now!

As far as I am aware, the submission process is robust against adversarial submissions. Everyone is invited to try to break it! (I will, of course, reset the leaderboard if you succeed, and publicly thank you for finding the problem.) Currently there is no authentication mechanism, so you can submit a solution under any "model" name; your Github username will be recorded with the solution. I can tighten this up if desired.

The intention of this eval is to encourage the development of models and frameworks that can effectively formalize material from the existing mathematical literature, including large developments that require substantial development of intermediate definitions and theorems in order to achieve the result. The eval does not make any attempt to directly encourage or require that this intermediate development is done well! I'm very open to suggestions about ways to do this that are compatible with automated evaluation. Mostly, however, I believe that sufficiently difficult problems simply can't be done without the capability to develop high quality intermediate theory, and hard evals will inevitably boost progress in this direction.

I'm aware that the problems in the eval are strongly skewed by the requirement that the problems can be stated with today's Mathlib. If you'd like to see more problems in other areas, please contribute to Mathlib!

I'm impressed that contractibility of Bing's house with two rooms has been solved in 7000+ lines by a Gemini/Claude ensemble with human in the loop using Antigravity ... Apparently it's also solved by Aleph Prover autonomously but the solution is not public?

From my reading of the proof: it divides the cuboid [0,4]x[0,3]x[0,2] into 24 cubes and fill them one at a time; the subspace after a filling deformation retracts onto the subspace before. Eventually when all cubes are filled we get the whole cuboid which is obviously contractible. This is a clever way to solve the problem and doesn't follow Hatcher's outline.

At four occasions the cube is retracted onto four of its faces, and at the remaining 20 occasions it's retracted onto five faces; the total number of faces added by the filling steps is 4x(6-4)+20x(6-5)=28. The 24 cubes have a total of (4+1)x3x2+4x(3+1)x2+4x3x(2+1)=98 faces. The house of two rooms have a total of 4x3x(2+1)-4 + 10 + 4x2x2+2x3x2 = 70 faces, and 70+28=98, which checks out.

I also asked it why the output is so large (100k LOC seems like a lot). It told me:

AI output

  • The pinned Mathlib did not have proper coherent-direct-image finiteness, relative Serre vanishing, Chow’s lemma, finite-cover Čech comparison, or even the later affine quasicoherent reconstruction API.
  • Consequently, the proof rebuilt a substantial algebraic-geometry stack: affine acyclicity, projective twist calculations, Serre finiteness, relative projective geometry, Chow graph closures, support thickening, and Noetherian support induction.
  • The benchmark’s target is not directly the usual vector-space-valued cohomology. It is ℚ ⊗[ℤ] M.sheaf.H n, with H defined through abelian-sheaf Ext. Bridging geometric ℚ-linear cohomology to that exact carrier required additional rationalization and change-of-scalars machinery.
  • Lean makes “canonical” chart, pullback, overlap, and base-change identifications explicit. The largest files illustrate this: effective sheaf-module descent is 3,370 lines, Segre chart-transition geometry 2,228, and Serre-twist overlap transitions 2,168.
  • The prohibition on increased heartbeats encouraged small helper lemmas and aggressive file splitting. That explains much of the 626-file count, although not the total LOC.

A meaningful portion was avoidable:
* 10,043 lines are not in the main theorem’s import closure.
* I overgeneralized several layers—arbitrary finite covers, general scalar cocycles, coefficient base change, and reusable relative-projective interfaces—beyond what the exact ℚ theorem required.
* Multiple attempted proof routes remained in the repository, including Mayer–Vietoris, Hilbert-series, and finite-subset machinery.
* The design introduced many “seam” modules: first stating conditional interfaces, then proving separate naturality and compatibility packages to discharge them.
* Even 96,897 is only a module-import closure. Imported modules can contain declarations the theorem never uses, so declaration-level pruning would find additional excess.

My assessment is that roughly 10k LOC is immediately and objectively removable. The remaining ~97k is a combination of genuinely missing library infrastructure and an overengineered low-level proof architecture. Reducing it substantially would require redesigning the proof and consolidating abstractions—not merely deleting extra files.
